title: I spy in two languages: a six-colour game for the living room
description: Classic I spy, played with colours instead of first letters so it works the same way in English and Spanish. Six colour words, one room, any time of day.
book_line: Bilingual English-Spanish vocabulary book for kids: themed word lists and simple activities, read on a Kindle, copied into a notebook when you want them on paper.
pin_title: I spy in two languages: a six-colour game for the living room
body:
I spy is usually played with first letters, and that is exactly what makes it awkward across two languages: the same object starts with a different letter in each. Play it with colours instead, and the game works the same way in English and in Spanish.

Six colours are enough to start: red, blue, green, yellow, white, black. In Spanish: rojo, azul, verde, amarillo, blanco, negro.

The opening line depends on the language you are building. For Spanish, the game has its own little call-and-response: "Veo, veo." "¿Qué ves?" "Algo verde." For English: "I spy with my little eye… something green."

Your child looks around and guesses by naming objects. They can guess in either language; when they use the other one, repeat the object in the language you are building and say yes or no: "¿El cojín? ¡Sí!" or "the cushion? Yes!".

Then swap: they spy, you guess. Guess wrong a few times on purpose. A child who gets to say "no, not that one" is running the conversation.

One grammar detail you can simply model: "algo" always takes the masculine form of the colour, so it is "algo rojo" and "algo blanco", never "algo roja". Once the object is named, the colour matches the object instead: la puerta roja, el cojín rojo.

Two variations for later. Add a second clue once colours are easy — "algo rojo y pequeño" / "something red and small". Or play on a walk, where the colours keep changing: a red door, a yellow flower, a white dog.

Keep the rounds quick. Five is plenty, and the best time is the waiting you already do: waiting for dinner, waiting for the bath to fill, waiting for a sibling to find their shoes.

What to avoid: stopping the game to correct a colour. If your child says the wrong colour word, just point to the object, say the right word in the language you are building, and carry on. The game keeps going, and they hear the word anyway.
